nodes.label: Heavy off-road machine
nodes.text: A heavy off-road machine is a very large, very heavy vehicle built to move earth, rock or materials on a job site rather than to travel on public roads.

nodes.label: Wheel loader
nodes.text: A wheel loader is a four-wheeled machine with a large bucket at the front that scoops up loose material and tips it into a truck or onto a pile.

nodes.label: Haul truck
nodes.text: A haul truck is a very large off-road dump truck that carries rock or ore from where it is dug to where it is dumped or processed.

nodes.label: Articulated hauler (ADT)
nodes.text: An articulated hauler, also called an articulated dump truck (ADT), is an off-road dump truck whose front and rear halves are joined by a hinge so it bends in the middle to steer.

nodes.label: Excavator
nodes.text: An excavator is a digging machine with a long jointed arm and a bucket, mounted on a body that can rotate a full circle on top of its tracks or wheels.

nodes.label: Dozer and grader
nodes.text: A dozer pushes earth and rock with a wide blade at the front, and a grader levels and shapes road surfaces with a long angled blade under its body.

nodes.label: Load-haul-dump machine (LHD)
nodes.text: A load-haul-dump machine (LHD) is a low, long loader built for underground mines, where it scoops broken rock, carries it along narrow tunnels and dumps it into a truck or a chute.

nodes.label: Trackless mobile machinery (TMM)
nodes.text: Trackless mobile machinery (TMM) is the South African legal term for any self-propelled mining machine that does not run on rails, from haul trucks and loaders to light vehicles.

nodes.label: Light vehicle
nodes.text: On a mine site, a light vehicle is an ordinary pickup, four-wheel-drive or van used by supervisors, maintenance crews and visitors to move among the heavy machines.

nodes.label: Operator and cab
nodes.text: The operator is the person who drives and controls a machine, and the cab is the enclosed compartment where that person sits.

nodes.label: Job site
nodes.text: A job site is any place where heavy machines work, and the booklet is concerned with four main kinds: surface mines, underground mines, quarries and construction sites.

nodes.label: Haul road, berm, bench and pit wall
nodes.text: These are the built features of a surface mine or quarry: the haul road is the internal road the trucks use, a berm is a ridge of material piled along an edge as a barrier, a bench is one horizontal step of the pit, and the pit wall is the steep face between benches.

nodes.label: Stockpile, dump point and tip point
nodes.text: A stockpile is a pile of loose material waiting to be used, a dump point is where a truck tips its load, and a tip point or tip head is the active edge of a dump where trucks and a dozer work together.

nodes.label: Spotter and pedestrian
nodes.text: A pedestrian is any person on foot near a working machine, and a spotter is a person whose job is to stand where the operator can see them and guide a reversing or maneuvering machine by hand signals or radio.

nodes.label: Blind spot and operator visibility
nodes.text: A blind spot is any area around a machine that the operator cannot see from the seat, and operator visibility is the overall picture of what the operator can and cannot see with eyes, mirrors and cameras.

nodes.label: Reversing and reverse alarm
nodes.text: Reversing (backing up) is driving a machine backward, and a reverse alarm is the loud beeping a machine makes automatically while it does so.

nodes.label: Vehicle interaction
nodes.text: Vehicle interaction is the mining industry's term for any situation in which a moving machine comes close to another machine, a person or a fixed feature of the site, whether or not contact happens.

nodes.label: Collision
nodes.text: A collision is a machine striking a person, a vehicle, another machine or a fixed object, and on job sites a small number of collision types cause most of the deaths.

nodes.label: Fatality, serious injury and property damage
nodes.text: Accidents are counted in three bands of severity, deaths, serious injuries and damage to equipment or structures, and the records get thinner and less reliable as severity goes down.

nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.text: Exposure is the amount of opportunity for something to happen, measured in units such as hours of machine operation, kilometers driven, loading cycles or number of close approaches, and it is the denominator that turns a count of events into a rate.

nodes.label: Near miss
nodes.text: A near miss is an event that could have caused a collision or injury but did not, usually because someone stopped, swerved or was lucky.

nodes.label: Collision Mitigation System (CMS)
nodes.text: A Collision Mitigation System (CMS) detects an object close to a machine, warns the operator, and if the operator does not react, applies the brakes automatically to avoid the collision or make it less severe.

nodes.label: Collision Warning System (CWS) and Collision Avoidance System (CAS)
nodes.text: A Collision Warning System (CWS) only alerts the operator to a nearby object, while a Collision Avoidance System (CAS) also acts on the machine, slowing or stopping it.

nodes.label: Proximity Detection System (PDS)
nodes.text: A Proximity Detection System (PDS) senses when a person or machine comes within a set distance of a machine and warns or stops it; the term is used mainly in US underground coal mining and in South Africa.

nodes.label: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) and Advanced Emergency Braking System (AEBS)
nodes.text: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB), called an Advanced Emergency Braking System (AEBS) in United Nations vehicle regulations, is the function on modern cars and trucks that brakes by itself when a crash with the vehicle or person ahead is about to happen.

nodes.label: Forward Collision Warning (FCW)
nodes.text: Forward Collision Warning (FCW) is the car and truck function that warns the driver of an imminent crash ahead but leaves the braking to the driver.

nodes.label: Pedestrian AEB (PAEB)
nodes.text: Pedestrian Automatic Emergency Braking (PAEB) is the version of car AEB that detects people on foot and brakes for them.

nodes.label: Intervention
nodes.text: An intervention is what a collision system does to the machine itself when the operator has not acted: it reduces speed, stops the machine, or prevents it from starting to move.

nodes.label: Staged intervention
nodes.text: Staged intervention means that a collision system acts in steps of increasing force, from a quiet information signal through warnings and gentle slowing to hard braking and a locked stop, rather than jumping straight to an emergency stop.

nodes.label: Nine levels of control
nodes.text: The nine levels of control are the mining industry's ladder of defenses against vehicle interactions, running from how a site is designed (Level 1) to a machine that brakes by itself (Level 9), with warning technology at Levels 7 and 8.

nodes.label: Nuisance braking
nodes.text: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, either because there was no real object (a false intervention) or because the object was real but posed no danger (an unnecessary intervention).

nodes.label: False alarm and alarm accuracy
nodes.text: A false alarm is a warning given when nothing dangerous is there, a nuisance alarm is a warning about something real that is not dangerous in the situation, and alarm accuracy is the share of all alarms that deserved a response.

nodes.label: Alarm fatigue
nodes.text: Alarm fatigue is the state in which a person has heard so many alarms that did not matter that they stop reacting to alarms at all, including the one that does matter.

nodes.label: Switching off and bypassing
nodes.text: Switching off and bypassing means defeating a safety system on purpose, by turning it off, overriding it, removing the tag it tracks, or redesigning its zones so it no longer protects what it should.

nodes.label: Operator reaction time
nodes.text: Operator reaction time is the time between a warning (or the appearance of a hazard) and the moment the operator begins to act, for example by pressing the brake.

nodes.label: Human factors
nodes.text: Human factors is the field that studies how people perceive, decide and act when working with machines, and designs the machine so that real people, tired or busy or distracted, can use it safely.

nodes.label: Human-machine interface (HMI)
nodes.text: The human-machine interface (HMI) is everything through which the system and the operator communicate: the screens, lights, sounds, vibrations and buttons in the cab.

nodes.label: Operator behavior change
nodes.text: Operator behavior change is the way people start to work differently once a protective system exists, including risk compensation (taking more risk because they feel protected) and over-reliance (letting the system do the watching).

nodes.label: Tasks that look like a collision risk to a sensor
nodes.text: Many normal, intended parts of the job, such as loading a truck, bumping a dump berm or working beside ground crew, put a large object close to the machine in exactly the way a sensor is designed to flag.

nodes.label: New risks created by automatic braking
nodes.text: An automatic stop can itself cause harm, through the jolt to the operator, a shifting or spilled load, loss of stability on a slope, a following machine running into the stopped one, or the machine rolling back once the brake is released.

nodes.label: Warning-system fleet
nodes.text: The warning-system fleet is the set of machines the manufacturer has already sold with the proximity warning system, and its field history is the record of what those machines have detected, warned about and got wrong in real use.

nodes.label: Sensor and prototype freeze
nodes.text: The sensor freeze is the project milestone at which the sensor types, numbers and mounting positions are fixed, and the prototype freeze is the milestone at which the first representative hardware and software are fixed; the booklet uses "before freeze" and "after freeze" to divide the work.

nodes.label: Validation window
nodes.text: The validation window is the period of less than four months after the prototype arrives in mid-2027 in which the Collision Mitigation System must be validated.

nodes.label: Site type and the "100+ site types" claim
nodes.text: A site type is a class of job site with a characteristic layout, surface and traffic (an open pit, a quarry face, a stockpile yard, a road works), and the "100+ site types" claim is the challenge statement that one machine may work across 100 or more job sites and applications.

nodes.label: Season and weather coverage
nodes.text: Season and weather coverage means making sure the system has been tested in all the conditions it will meet, including rain, snow, fog, dust, mud, glare, dusk and darkness, and the problem is that the validation window falls in a season that contains few of them.

nodes.label: Hazard, harm and risk
nodes.text: A hazard is something that could hurt someone, harm is the injury or damage that actually happens, and risk is how likely the harm is, combined with how bad it would be.

nodes.label: Hazard analysis and risk assessment
nodes.text: Hazard analysis is the organized search for everything about a machine and its use that could cause harm, and risk assessment is the judgment of how likely and how severe each of those harms would be.

nodes.label: Safety function and safety-related control system
nodes.text: A safety function is one specific job that a machine's control system must do to keep people safe, and the safety-related control system is the chain of parts (sensor, computer, actuator) that performs that job.

nodes.label: Functional safety
nodes.text: Functional safety is the part of safety that depends on a control system doing the right thing at the right time, including when its own parts fail.

nodes.label: Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF)
nodes.text: SOTIF is the part of safety concerned with a system that has no broken parts yet still behaves unsafely, because its sensing or decision-making is not good enough for the situation it meets.

nodes.label: Performance Level (PL) and Category
nodes.text: A Performance Level is a five-step grade, written a to e, that says how reliably a safety function on a machine must work, and the Category describes the circuit architecture used to reach that grade.

nodes.label: Machine Performance Level (MPL)
nodes.text: The Machine Performance Level is the earth-moving-machinery version of the Performance Level, defined in the ISO 19014 series, with a required level (MPLr) set by hazard analysis and an achieved level (MPLa) demonstrated by the design.

nodes.label: Safety Integrity Level (SIL)
nodes.text: A Safety Integrity Level is a grade from 1 to 4 used in the IEC 61508 family of standards to say how much risk reduction a safety function must deliver, and the same three letters are used in this booklet for software-in-the-loop, a completely different thing.

nodes.label: Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL)
nodes.text: ASIL is the road-vehicle grading of how demanding a safety requirement is, from A (lowest) to D (highest), defined in ISO 26262, and it does not apply by scope to off-road machines.

nodes.label: Fail-safe, safe state, controlled stop and emergency stop
nodes.text: A fail-safe system moves itself to a safe state when something goes wrong, and for a moving machine that safe state is usually reached by a controlled stop or, when time is short, an emergency stop.

nodes.label: Fault, failure, failure mode and fault injection
nodes.text: A fault is a defect inside a system, a failure is the moment the system stops doing its job because of a fault, a failure mode is the particular way it fails, and fault injection is deliberately introducing faults to see how the system responds.

nodes.label: FMEA, FMECA and FMEDA
nodes.text: These are three related table-based methods that go through a system part by part and ask, for each part, how it could fail, what would happen, how serious that would be and, in the FMEDA, whether the system would notice.

nodes.label: Fault tree analysis (FTA)
nodes.text: A fault tree starts from one unwanted top event and works downward, drawing the combinations of smaller failures that could cause it, joined by AND and OR logic.

nodes.label: Common-cause failure and independence of channels
nodes.text: A common-cause failure is one event that knocks out two or more parts that were supposed to back each other up, so redundancy only counts when the channels are truly independent.

nodes.label: Diagnostic coverage and dead time of a safety function
nodes.text: Diagnostic coverage is the share of dangerous faults that the system can detect by itself, and dead time is any period during which the safety function is not actually protecting anyone, because a fault has not yet been noticed or because the function is degraded or switched off.

nodes.label: Residual risk and as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP)
nodes.text: Residual risk is the risk that remains after all the protective measures are in place, and ALARP is the principle that risk must be reduced until the cost of reducing it further would be grossly out of proportion to the benefit gained.
aliases: Residual risk and as low as reasonably practicable

nodes.label: Acceptance criteria and pass or fail criteria
nodes.text: Acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions, agreed before testing starts, that decide whether a result is good enough, and pass or fail criteria are the same idea applied to one test.

nodes.label: Requirements and requirements-based testing
nodes.text: A requirement is a written statement of what the system must do, precise enough to be tested, and requirements-based testing means that every test exists to check a named requirement and every requirement has at least one test.

nodes.label: Traceability
nodes.text: Traceability is an unbroken written chain of links from each safety claim to the requirement it rests on, to the scenarios and tests that check that requirement, to the recorded evidence, so that anyone can follow the chain in either direction.

nodes.label: Verification versus validation (V&V)
nodes.text: Verification asks "did we build the thing correctly, according to its specification?", validation asks "did we build the right thing, one that works in the real world for its intended use?", and V&V is the pair.

nodes.label: The V-model of development
nodes.text: The V-model is a picture of a development process shaped like the letter V: the left arm breaks the need down into requirements and designs, the bottom is where the parts are built, and the right arm climbs back up through tests that check each level against the level opposite it.

nodes.label: Safety case and safety argument
nodes.text: A safety case is a structured written argument, supported by evidence, that a system is acceptably safe for a stated use in a stated environment, and the safety argument is the reasoning that connects the evidence to the claim.

nodes.label: Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) and Structured Assurance Case Metamodel (SACM)
nodes.text: GSN is a standard set of diagram shapes for drawing a safety argument, and SACM is a formal data model that lets software tools store and exchange such arguments.

nodes.label: Assurance case for autonomous products (UL 4600)
nodes.text: UL 4600 is a standard that explains how to build and judge a safety case for a product that makes decisions on its own, by setting out a long list of topics and questions the case must answer.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.text: Evidence is any recorded fact (a test result, a measurement, a field record, an analysis, a document) that supports or weakens a claim, and its strength depends on who produced it, how independently, and how directly it bears on the claim.

nodes.label: Independent assessment, independent test body and safety board
nodes.text: Independent assessment is a review of the safety evidence by people who did not produce it; an independent test body is an outside organization that runs or witnesses tests; and a safety board is the internal group with the authority to accept or reject the safety case.

nodes.label: Evidence gate and decision gate
nodes.text: A decision gate is a planned point at which management must decide whether a program continues, changes course or stops, and an evidence gate is a decision gate whose pass criterion is a piece of evidence obtained, not a date reached.

nodes.label: Staged release and limited operating domain
nodes.text: Staged release means switching the automatic brake on first only for a narrow, well-understood set of machines, movements, speeds and conditions (the limited operating domain), and widening that set step by step as evidence from the field arrives.

nodes.label: Field monitoring and operational monitoring
nodes.text: Field monitoring, also called operational or in-service monitoring, is the planned collection and review of data from machines in real use after release, to check that the system behaves as the safety case predicted and to catch the problems the tests missed.

nodes.label: Proven in use and reuse of evidence
nodes.text: "Proven in use" is a formal route in the functional-safety standards for trusting a component because it has already worked reliably for a long time in the same conditions, and reuse of evidence is the broader idea of carrying test results and analyses from one machine model or product to another instead of repeating them.

nodes.label: Equivalence argument between machine variants
nodes.text: An equivalence argument, also called a similarity argument, is the reasoned and evidenced claim that evidence gathered on one machine variant also holds for another, because the differences between them do not affect the safety-relevant behavior.

nodes.label: Safety of machinery (ISO 12100)
nodes.text: ISO 12100 is the foundation standard for machine safety: it defines the basic words (hazard, risk, protective measure) and sets out the general method for reducing machine risk in a fixed order.

nodes.label: Electro-sensitive protective equipment (ESPE) and safety-related sensors
nodes.text: ESPE is the family of certified safety sensors (light curtains, laser scanners and, recently, radar) that detect a person without touching them and trigger a protective stop, and IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 are the standards that define how such sensors are shown to be reliable.

nodes.label: Machine learning in safety functions
nodes.text: Machine learning (ML) is software whose behavior is learned from examples rather than written as explicit rules, and when such software helps decide whether to brake, safety engineers treat it differently because its rules cannot be read, its failures are hard to predict, and the standards for it are still being written.

nodes.label: Product liability and the EU Product Liability Directive (PLD)
nodes.text: Product liability is the legal duty of a manufacturer to compensate people harmed by a defective product, and the European Union's new Product Liability Directive extends that duty explicitly to software and makes it easier for claimants to obtain the manufacturer's internal evidence.
aliases: Product liability and the EU Product Liability Directive

nodes.label: Red team and hostile review
nodes.text: A red team is a group given the explicit job of attacking a plan to find its weaknesses before real reviewers, customers or accidents do, and a hostile review is the same stance applied to a document.

nodes.label: Failure mode of a project and early warning sign
nodes.text: Borrowing the engineering word, a failure mode of a project is one specific way the project could fail to deliver what it promised, and an early warning sign is an observable symptom that appears while there is still time to act.

nodes.label: Fallback option
nodes.text: A fallback option is a pre-planned, less ambitious but still responsible outcome that the program switches to when the main plan cannot be delivered on time, chosen so that safety is preserved rather than the headline schedule.

nodes.label: Sensor
nodes.text: A sensor is a device that measures something about the world, such as distance, light or speed, and turns the measurement into an electrical signal a computer can read.

nodes.label: Perception
nodes.text: Perception is the chain of steps by which a machine turns raw sensor signals into a short list of the things around it, with positions and speeds, that the braking logic can act on.

nodes.label: Detection, classification and tracking
nodes.text: Detection says "something is there", classification says "it is a person" or "it is a truck", and tracking follows the object over time so the system knows where it is going; the result is written down as an object list.

nodes.label: Field of view (FOV), range, resolution and frame rate (FPS)
nodes.text: These four numbers describe how much a sensor can see: how wide (field of view), how far (range), in how much detail (resolution) and how often (frame rate).

nodes.label: Latency
nodes.text: Latency is the delay between the moment something happens in front of the machine and the moment the machine reacts, measured in a braking system from sensing to the brake command and on to actual deceleration.

nodes.label: Camera (RGB camera, CMOS sensor, lens, image signal processor ISP, HDR, rolling shutter)
nodes.text: A camera collects visible light through a lens onto a grid of light-sensitive cells and produces a color image that a computer can search for people and objects.

nodes.label: Image quality terms: modulation transfer function (MTF), point spread function (PSF), noise, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)
nodes.text: These measures say how sharp and how clean a sensor's picture is, so that a simulated camera can be checked against a real one.

nodes.label: Stereo camera and depth camera (RGB-D)
nodes.text: A stereo camera uses two cameras a known distance apart to work out how far away things are, and a depth camera (RGB-D) delivers a color image plus a distance for every pixel.

nodes.label: Lidar (light detection and ranging)
nodes.text: A lidar sends out very short laser pulses, times how long each takes to bounce back, and so builds a precise three-dimensional map of distances around the machine.

nodes.label: Point cloud
nodes.text: A point cloud is a large set of measured points in three-dimensional space, each with an x, y and z position and often a brightness value, that together outline the shapes around a sensor.

nodes.label: Radar (radio detection and ranging)
nodes.text: A radar sends out radio waves and listens for their echoes, measuring both the distance to objects and, from a shift in the returned frequency, how fast they approach or recede.

nodes.label: Ultrasonic sensor
nodes.text: An ultrasonic sensor sends out a short burst of sound too high for people to hear and measures the echo to find the distance to the nearest object within a few meters.

nodes.label: Thermal camera (long-wave infrared, LWIR, NETD)
nodes.text: A thermal camera makes an image from the heat that objects give off, so it can show a warm person against cold ground in complete darkness.

nodes.label: Tag-based proximity systems (UWB, RFID, magnetic field)
nodes.text: A tag-based proximity system does not look for people and objects; it listens for a small electronic tag that each person or vehicle carries, and warns or stops when a tag comes too close.

nodes.label: Satellite positioning (GNSS, GPS, RTK) and inertial sensing (IMU, INS)
nodes.text: Satellite positioning tells a machine where it is on the earth, inertial sensing tells it how it is moving and turning from moment to moment, and together they give the position and motion to which every other measurement is referred.

nodes.label: Sensor fusion
nodes.text: Sensor fusion is the combining of measurements from several different sensors into one picture of the surroundings that is more reliable than any single sensor could give.

nodes.label: Calibration (intrinsic and extrinsic) and sensor mounting
nodes.text: Calibration is the measurement of how a sensor sees (its internal, intrinsic properties) and where it sits on the machine (its external, extrinsic position and angle), so that its readings can be placed correctly in the real world.

nodes.label: Time synchronization and time stamps
nodes.text: A time stamp is the exact time written next to each measurement, and time synchronization is making sure every sensor and computer on the machine writes those times from the same clock.

nodes.label: Sensor degradation: dust, mud, rain, snow, fog, spray, glare, darkness, artificial lighting, vibration
nodes.text: Sensor degradation is the loss of a sensor's performance when the environment interferes with it, by blocking its view, dirtying its window, flooding it with light or shaking it.

nodes.label: Occlusion (hidden objects) and sensor obstruction (blocked sensor)
nodes.text: Occlusion is when an object is hidden behind something else so the sensor cannot see it, and obstruction is when the sensor itself is blocked, for example by mud on its window.

nodes.label: Cluttered and reflective surroundings
nodes.text: Cluttered and reflective surroundings are environments full of metal, water, walls and piles that bounce sensor signals in confusing ways, producing echoes from nowhere and hiding real objects.

nodes.label: Ground truth
nodes.text: Ground truth is the trusted, independent record of what was really in front of the machine, where and when, against which the system's detections and warnings are scored.

nodes.label: Labeling and annotation (human labels, auto-labeling, offboard detectors)
nodes.text: Labeling, or annotation, is the work of marking what is in recorded sensor data, such as drawing a box around each person and naming it, so that detectors can be trained and their results scored.

nodes.label: Datasets and benchmarks (what MOCS, SODA, RELLIS-3D, RUGD and similar names are)
nodes.text: A dataset is a large collection of recorded and labeled sensor data that researchers share, and a benchmark is a dataset plus an agreed scoring rule, so that different methods can be compared on the same test.

nodes.label: True positive, false positive, false negative, miss (the four outcomes)
nodes.text: Every time a detector looks for something, one of four things happens: it finds something real (true positive), it reports something that is not there (false positive), it misses something real (false negative, or miss), or it correctly stays quiet (true negative).
aliases: True positive, false positive, false negative, miss

nodes.label: True positive rate, precision, recall, F1 score
nodes.text: These single numbers summarize the four outcomes: recall (the true positive rate) is the share of real objects that were found, precision is the share of reports that were real, and the F1 score blends the two.

nodes.label: ROC curve and DET curve
nodes.text: A ROC curve and a DET curve are graphs that show how a detector's misses and false alarms trade against each other as its sensitivity setting is turned up or down.

nodes.label: Time to collision (TTC) and trigger distance (as perception outputs that matter for braking)
nodes.text: Time to collision is how many seconds remain before the machine and an object meet if neither changes speed, and trigger distance is how far away an object must be when the system decides to warn or brake; both are only as good as the distance and speed that perception delivers.

nodes.label: Machine learning detector (neural network, convolutional neural network CNN, training data, inference)
nodes.text: A machine learning detector is software that has learned to find people and objects in sensor data by being shown many labeled examples, instead of being programmed with hand-written rules.

nodes.label: Training data, validation data, test data, and the independence rule (data lineage)
nodes.text: Machine-learning data are split into three parts, one to teach the detector, one to choose its settings and one to score it honestly, and the independence rule says the scoring data must never have touched the teaching.
aliases: Training data, validation data, test data, and the independence rule

nodes.label: Synthetic and generated training data (domain gap, data augmentation)
nodes.text: Synthetic training data are sensor data made by a simulator or a generative model rather than recorded in the field, and the domain gap is the difference between that artificial data and real data that makes a detector trained on one do worse on the other.

nodes.label: Generative models (GAN, diffusion models) and what "generated weather" means
nodes.text: Generative models are machine-learning systems that create new, realistic-looking images or sensor data, and "generated weather" means using them to add rain, fog, snow, dust or night to a recording made in clear weather.

nodes.label: Neural rendering: NeRF and Gaussian splatting (3DGS) as ways to rebuild a scene from photos
nodes.text: Neural rendering takes many photographs or scans of a real place and learns a model of it that can then produce new views from positions where no camera ever stood.

nodes.label: Physically based rendering (PBR), BRDF and BSDF (how materials reflect light and radar)
nodes.text: Physically based rendering computes what a sensor sees from the real physics of light and materials, and a BRDF or BSDF is the mathematical description of how a given surface sends incoming energy back out in each direction.

nodes.label: Ray tracing and shooting-and-bouncing rays (SBR) for sensor simulation
nodes.text: Ray tracing simulates a sensor by following imaginary rays of light, radio or sound from the sensor into the virtual scene, bouncing them off surfaces and recording what comes back; shooting-and-bouncing rays is the radar version that launches very many rays and adds up their reflections.

nodes.label: Electronic control unit (ECU)
nodes.text: An electronic control unit is one of the small, rugged computers built into a machine, each running one job such as controlling the engine, the brakes or, here, the collision system.

nodes.label: Vehicle network: CAN bus, SAE J1939, DBC file
nodes.text: The vehicle network is the wiring and message system through which a machine's computers talk to one another, and J1939 is the standard dialect heavy machines use on it, including for the message that asks the machine to slow or stop.

nodes.label: Data logging (what to record on the machine, raw versus processed data, common mistakes)
nodes.text: Data logging is recording what the machine's sensors saw, what the machine did and what the system decided, in enough detail that the whole event can be replayed and judged later.
aliases: what to record on the machine

nodes.label: Data formats and versioning (MDF, CSV, YAML, XML, JSON, Robot Operating System ROS bags)
nodes.text: A data format is the agreed way a file is laid out so that software can read it, and versioning is the practice of giving every file, setting and program a unique identifier so that any result can be traced back to exactly what produced it.

nodes.label: Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC)
nodes.text: Electromagnetic compatibility is the ability of a piece of electronics to work correctly amid electrical noise from other equipment and to avoid producing noise that disturbs others.

nodes.label: Over-the-air (OTA) sensor stimulation (as a sensor concept)
nodes.text: Over-the-air sensor stimulation means presenting an artificial signal, a radio echo, a projected image, a laser return or a sound, to a real sensor's own antenna or lens so that the sensor believes it is seeing a real scene.

nodes.label: Model and model fidelity
nodes.text: A model is a simplified description of a real thing, written in mathematics or computer code, that behaves like the real thing closely enough to answer one particular question, and its fidelity is how closely it does so.

nodes.label: Simulation and simulator
nodes.text: A simulation is a computer run in which models of the machine, the site, the sensors and the people act together over time, and a simulator is the software that runs it.

nodes.label: Virtual validation (virtual testing)
nodes.text: Virtual validation means collecting evidence that a system meets its safety requirements by testing it in simulation and on laboratory benches instead of, or before, testing the complete real machine.

nodes.label: Physics-based versus data-driven models
nodes.text: A physics-based model computes what happens from the laws of nature, while a data-driven model learns what usually happens from recorded examples.

nodes.label: Digital twin
nodes.text: A digital twin is a detailed computer model of one specific real machine or site, kept matched to the real thing by measurements.

nodes.label: Virtual job site (virtual environment, scene, 3D asset)
nodes.text: A virtual job site is a three-dimensional computer model of a mine, quarry or construction site in which simulated machines, sensors and people can be tested.

nodes.label: Terrain model, digital elevation model (DEM), mesh and collision proxy
nodes.text: A terrain model describes the shape of the ground, a digital elevation model (DEM) is its simplest form, a mesh is the surface of small triangles that a computer draws, and a collision proxy is the invisible simplified shape used to detect contact.

nodes.label: Photogrammetry, laser scanning and SLAM
nodes.text: These are three ways of measuring a real site in three dimensions: from overlapping photographs, from laser distance measurements, or from a moving machine's own sensors as it drives.

nodes.label: Structure from motion (COLMAP) and scene reconstruction
nodes.text: Structure from motion is the mathematical method that recovers camera positions and a three-dimensional point cloud from ordinary photographs, COLMAP is a widely used free program that does it, and scene reconstruction is the whole process of turning recordings into a usable virtual site.

nodes.label: Procedural generation
nodes.text: Procedural generation builds many different virtual sites automatically from rules and parameter ranges instead of modeling each site by hand.

nodes.label: Game engine (Unreal Engine, Unity)
nodes.text: A game engine is the software core of a video game, which draws three-dimensional worlds, moves objects with simple physics and runs in real time, and many sensor simulators are built on one.

nodes.label: Material and sensor material (ASAM OpenMATERIAL)
nodes.text: In simulation, a material is the description of how a surface responds to light, radio waves or sound, and ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D is a standard format for storing those properties for camera, lidar and radar.

nodes.label: Scene description standards: OpenUSD, OpenDRIVE, OpenCRG, OpenSCENARIO, OpenLABEL, OpenODD, OpenXOntology
nodes.text: These are agreed file formats that let different simulation tools exchange the same description of a world, a road, a road surface, a sequence of events, a set of labels, an operating domain or a shared vocabulary.

nodes.label: Open Simulation Interface (ASAM OSI) and the ASAM organization
nodes.text: ASAM OSI is a standard set of messages that lets an environment model, a sensor model and the function under test talk to each other during a simulation, and ASAM is the industry association that publishes it.

nodes.label: Co-simulation, Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI), Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU) and SSP
nodes.text: Co-simulation runs several separate simulation programs together in step, FMI is the standard that lets them plug into each other, an FMU is one model packaged to that standard, and SSP describes how a set of FMUs is wired together.

nodes.label: Operational design domain (ODD) and operating-domain taxonomy
nodes.text: The operational design domain is the written description of the conditions under which a system is designed to work, and an operating-domain taxonomy is the organized list of attributes used to write it.

nodes.label: Scenario (functional, logical, concrete)
nodes.text: A scenario is a description of a situation that unfolds over time, written at one of three levels of detail: in words (functional), with parameter ranges (logical), or with every value fixed (concrete).

nodes.label: Scenario catalog, scenario family and scenario parameter
nodes.text: A scenario catalog is the complete, traceable list of situations a system must be tested against, a scenario family is one logical scenario with its parameter ranges and probability distribution, and a scenario parameter is one of the variables in that family.

nodes.label: Test case, test matrix and scenario grid
nodes.text: A test case is one fully specified test with an expected result, a test matrix is a table of test cases arranged by the factors they vary, and a scenario grid is a matrix whose cells are concrete scenarios.

nodes.label: Corner case, edge case and rare event
nodes.text: An edge case sits at the limit of one parameter, a corner case sits at the limits of several at once, and a rare event is a situation that happens so seldom in normal operation that waiting for it is not a practical way to test it.

nodes.label: The X-in-the-loop family (MIL, SIL, HIL, PIL, VIL, DIL)
nodes.text: "X-in-the-loop" names a family of test setups in which one real part of the system (the X) is connected to a simulation of everything else, and the family forms a ladder from all-virtual to all-real.

nodes.label: Model-in-the-loop (MIL)
nodes.text: Model-in-the-loop testing runs a model of the control logic against a model of the machine and its surroundings, with no real software or hardware yet.

nodes.label: Software-in-the-loop (SIL)
nodes.text: Software-in-the-loop testing runs the real braking software, compiled for an ordinary computer, inside a simulated machine on a simulated site, so that thousands of scenarios can be tried without any hardware.

nodes.label: Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) with data injection
nodes.text: Hardware-in-the-loop testing connects the real electronic control unit, with its real wiring and network messages, to a simulator that runs in real time and feeds it the data a real machine would produce.

nodes.label: Direct digital or raw signal injection
nodes.text: Raw signal injection feeds simulated or recorded sensor data into the sensor's electronics at a defined electrical point, so that everything downstream of that point is tested and everything upstream is not.

nodes.label: Over-the-air sensor stimulation (sensor-in-the-loop)
nodes.text: Over-the-air stimulation presents a real, complete sensor with artificial light, radio waves or sound generated from the virtual scene, so that the whole sensor, including its optics or antenna and its firmware, is in the loop.

nodes.label: Vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL) and mixed reality
nodes.text: Vehicle-in-the-loop testing drives the complete real machine on a safe, empty test area while virtual hazards are fed to its sensors or controller, so that it brakes for a worker who exists only in the simulation.

nodes.label: Driver-in-the-loop (DIL), operator-in-the-loop and the machine simulator
nodes.text: Driver-in-the-loop or operator-in-the-loop testing puts a real person in a simulator cab, with screens, controls and sometimes motion, to study how operators react when the machine warns, waits and then brakes.

nodes.label: Real time (hard real time)
nodes.text: A simulation runs in real time when one simulated second takes exactly one real second, and in hard real time when every computing step is guaranteed to finish within its deadline, every time.

nodes.label: Open loop versus closed loop
nodes.text: In an open-loop test the system's output does not change what happens next, while in a closed-loop test the system's actions feed back and alter the situation it then sees.

nodes.label: Replay and re-simulation of recorded data (open-loop replay)
nodes.text: Replay feeds sensor data recorded on real machines back into the software, exactly as recorded, to see what the software would have detected and decided.
aliases: Replay and re-simulation of recorded data

nodes.label: Semantic or object-list replay
nodes.text: Semantic replay feeds the decision software not with raw sensor data but with a list of objects (type, position, speed), either recorded or taken from ground truth, so that only the warning and braking logic is tested.

nodes.label: Shadow mode (silent testing)
nodes.text: In shadow mode the new braking software runs live on working machines, sees everything the sensors see and decides when it would brake, but its brake commands are disconnected, so it only records what it would have done.

nodes.label: Proving ground, track test and whole-machine test
nodes.text: A proving ground is a closed, controlled area where the complete real machine, with its real sensors, is tested against physical targets; a track test is one such test, and a whole-machine test is any test in which nothing is simulated.

nodes.label: Soft target, robotic target and target platform (ISO 19206)
nodes.text: A soft target is a dummy of a person or vehicle that a machine can hit without damage, a robotic target or target platform is a low, self-driving carrier that moves the dummy along a programmed path, and ISO 19206 is the standard series that specifies such targets for road-vehicle testing.
aliases: Soft target, robotic target and target platform

nodes.label: Correlation test
nodes.text: A correlation test is a physical test run specifically to check whether the models predicted what the real machine did, and by how much they were wrong.

nodes.label: Regression testing and continuous integration (CI/CD) for simulation
nodes.text: Regression testing re-runs old tests after every software change to make sure that nothing which used to work now fails, and continuous integration is the automated factory that does this on every change.

nodes.label: Test management, versioning and the traceability chain
nodes.text: Test management is the record-keeping that lets thousands of runs be planned, reproduced and traced from the hazard they address to the evidence they produce, and versioning gives every ingredient of a run a fixed identifier.

nodes.label: Cloud execution and compute budget
nodes.text: Cloud execution means renting computers by the hour from a data-center provider to run many simulations in parallel, and the compute budget is the money and machine-hours set aside for that.

nodes.label: Headless simulation versus rendered simulation
nodes.text: A headless simulation runs without drawing any picture, computing only the numbers a test needs, while a rendered simulation produces images or sensor views, which costs far more computing.

nodes.label: Sim-to-real gap
nodes.text: The sim-to-real gap is the difference between what a system does in simulation and what it does in reality, caused by everything the models leave out or get wrong.

nodes.label: Domain randomization
nodes.text: Domain randomization deliberately varies the appearance and conditions of simulated scenes at random (lighting, colors, textures, object positions) so that software trained or tested on them does not depend on details that will differ in reality.

nodes.label: "Do not make one simulator carry every test" (multi-simulator architecture)
nodes.text: This is the booklet's recommendation to spread the test program across several levels of simulation fidelity and several tools, each used for the questions it answers well, instead of running every case in one maximum-fidelity simulator.
aliases: "Do not make one simulator carry every test"

nodes.label: Mass, payload and gross vehicle weight (GVWR)
nodes.text: Mass is how much matter a machine contains, payload is the load it carries, and the gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) is the maximum total of machine plus load that the manufacturer allows.
aliases: Mass, payload and gross vehicle weight

nodes.label: Speed, acceleration and deceleration
nodes.text: Speed is how fast something moves, acceleration is how quickly its speed increases, and deceleration is how quickly its speed decreases.

nodes.label: Stopping distance
nodes.text: Stopping distance is how far a machine travels from the moment a stop becomes necessary until it stands still.

nodes.label: Brake dead time and brake build-up time
nodes.text: Brake dead time is the pause between the brake command and the first braking effect, and build-up time is the further period until the brakes reach their full force.

nodes.label: End-to-end latency budget
nodes.text: The end-to-end latency budget is the list of every delay between an object appearing and the machine standing still, with a time allowance for each.

nodes.label: Grade (slope) and its effect on braking
nodes.text: Grade is the steepness of the ground; going downhill reduces how hard a machine can slow down, and going uphill helps it.

nodes.label: Surface and traction
nodes.text: Traction is the grip between a tire or track and the ground, and on loose, wet or soft surfaces there is less of it, so braking is limited by the ground rather than by the brakes.

nodes.label: Wheels versus tracks
nodes.text: Wheeled machines roll on rubber tires, tracked or crawler machines run on steel or rubber belts, and the two grip, steer and stop differently.

nodes.label: Articulated steering
nodes.text: Articulated steering turns a machine by bending it at a hinge between its front and rear halves, which suits rough ground but makes the machine swing and pitch when it brakes.

nodes.label: Hydrostatic drive, retarder and service brake
nodes.text: Heavy machines slow down in three ways: with friction brakes (the service brake), with a retarder that uses the drivetrain to hold speed on long descents, and on many machines with a hydrostatic drive that brakes by itself when the operator eases off.

nodes.label: Load shift and stability
nodes.text: Stability is a machine's resistance to tipping, sliding or losing control, and hard braking is itself a hazard because it throws the load forward and can push the machine past its limits.

nodes.label: Vehicle dynamics model
nodes.text: A vehicle dynamics model is a set of equations that predicts how a machine moves, slows, turns, leans and pitches in response to brake, drive and steering inputs.

nodes.label: Tire model and tire-soil interaction
nodes.text: A tire model is a formula or table that gives the forward, braking and sideways force a tire produces for a given load, slip and surface; tire-soil interaction is the harder case where the ground deforms under the tire.

nodes.label: Terramechanics (SCM, DEM, SPH, CRM, FEM)
nodes.text: Terramechanics is the science of how wheels and tracks interact with soil, and SCM, DEM, SPH, CRM and FEM are five ways of computing that interaction, from a fast approximate formula to very slow grain-by-grain simulation.

nodes.label: Brake model and powertrain model
nodes.text: A brake model predicts how much braking force arrives, and how quickly, after a command; a powertrain model predicts how the engine, transmission and drive add to or fight that braking.

nodes.label: Model fidelity levels for braking
nodes.text: Model fidelity is how much physical detail a model includes; for braking, the levels run from a lookup table or single formula, through a point-mass model with measured delays, to a full multibody simulation with soil.

nodes.label: Physical tests needed to build and check a braking model
nodes.text: These are the measurements on a real machine that give a braking model its numbers (calibration) and then show whether its predictions hold on cases it has not seen (validation).

nodes.label: Decision logic (when to warn, when to brake)
nodes.text: Decision logic is the set of rules inside the system that turns "there is an object over there" into "do nothing", "warn the operator" or "apply the brakes".

nodes.label: Time to collision (TTC), time headway and trigger distance
nodes.text: Time to collision is how many seconds remain before two things meet if nothing changes, time headway is how many seconds the machine needs to reach the spot an object occupies now, and trigger distance is the range at which the system must act.

nodes.label: Zones (warning zone, braking zone, detection zone)
nodes.text: Zones are areas drawn around the machine in which the system reacts in a particular way: it must see objects anywhere in the detection zone, it warns when one enters the warning zone, and it brakes when one enters the braking zone.

nodes.label: Thresholds and filters
nodes.text: Thresholds are the numbers at which the system changes its behavior, and filters are the rules that stop it from reacting to a single noisy measurement.

nodes.label: Staged interventions in the decision logic
nodes.text: Staged intervention means the system escalates step by step, from information to warning to slowing to partial braking to maximum safe braking and, for a stationary machine, to refusing to move, rather than jumping straight to a full stop.

nodes.label: Deceleration limits and how regulators specify them
nodes.text: A deceleration limit is a rule about how hard a machine must, or may, slow down, and regulators write such rules in several different and not directly comparable ways.

nodes.label: Operator-already-reacting detection
nodes.text: This is the part of the logic that notices the operator is already braking or steering away, so the machine does not brake on top of a person who is handling the situation.

nodes.label: Nuisance braking from the decision side
nodes.text: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, and "from the decision side" means the cases where the sensors saw something real but the logic should have known not to brake.

nodes.label: Required detection range
nodes.text: The required detection range is how far the sensors must reliably see, worked out backwards from how far the machine needs to stop plus a safety margin.

nodes.label: Residual safe distance
nodes.text: Residual safe distance is the gap deliberately left between the stopped machine and the object, so that a stop is a near miss and not a light touch.

nodes.label: Secondary hazards of an automatic stop
nodes.text: Secondary hazards are the new dangers an automatic stop creates by itself: being struck from behind, blocking an escape route, stalling or rolling back on a grade, spilling the load, or hurting the operator.

nodes.label: Mixed motion and prediction of movement
nodes.text: Mixed motion is the case where both the machine and the person or vehicle are moving, so the system must predict where each will be, not just where they are now.

nodes.label: Tuning thresholds in simulation before field tests
nodes.text: Tuning in simulation means adjusting the decision thresholds, zone sizes and filters on a computer model of machine, sensors and site, so that field tests confirm settings rather than discover them.

nodes.label: Test space and the combinatorial explosion
nodes.text: The test space is the set of every situation the braking system could meet, and the combinatorial explosion is the way that set grows so fast, when conditions are multiplied together, that nobody can test it all.

nodes.label: Parameter, parameter range and parameterized scenario family
nodes.text: A parameter is one adjustable quantity in a test (such as machine speed), its range is the span of values it may take, and a parameterized scenario family is one scenario description with those quantities left open so that thousands of concrete tests can be generated from it.

nodes.label: Test selection method
nodes.text: A test selection method is a rule for choosing which of the countless possible tests to actually run, and each rule can honestly answer only certain kinds of question.

nodes.label: Design of experiments (DOE)
nodes.text: Design of experiments (DOE) is the branch of statistics that plans which combinations of settings to test so that the effect of each factor, and of factors acting together, can be measured with the fewest runs.
aliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology

nodes.label: Combinatorial testing (t-way testing, pairwise testing, covering arrays)
nodes.text: Combinatorial testing chooses a small set of tests that still guarantees every combination of values of any t factors (for pairwise testing, any two) appears at least once.

nodes.label: Random sampling, stratified sampling and probability-weighted sampling
nodes.text: Random sampling picks tests by chance according to how often each situation occurs in real operation, stratified sampling first divides the situations into groups (strata) and samples each group deliberately, and probability-weighted sampling keeps track of each test's real-world frequency so that results can be scaled back to the field.

nodes.label: Space-filling designs (Latin hypercube)
nodes.text: A space-filling design spreads test points as evenly as possible across the ranges of several continuous parameters at once, so that no region of the space is left unexplored.

nodes.label: Falsification (failure-seeking search)
nodes.text: Falsification is a test method that treats "find a case where the system fails" as a search problem and uses optimization to steer the simulator toward the most dangerous combinations of conditions.

nodes.label: Rare-event methods (importance sampling)
nodes.text: Rare-event methods deliberately make dangerous situations happen more often in simulation, then mathematically correct the results so that the estimated rate still refers to normal operation.

nodes.label: Adaptive and Bayesian test selection
nodes.text: Adaptive test selection chooses each new test based on the results of the tests so far, often using a Bayesian model that keeps track of what is still uncertain.

nodes.label: Monte Carlo methods
nodes.text: A Monte Carlo method answers a question by running the same experiment many times with randomly chosen inputs and counting what happens.

nodes.label: Sample size, confidence level and confidence interval
nodes.text: The sample size is how many independent trials you run, the confidence level is how sure you want to be, and the confidence interval is the range of values for the true rate that the data support at that level of sureness.

nodes.label: Binomial claims and the rule of three
nodes.text: A binomial claim is a statement about the probability of a yes-or-no outcome (detected or missed) based on a count of trials, and the rule of three is the shortcut that says: with zero failures in n trials, you can be about 95 percent confident that the true failure probability is below 3 divided by n.

nodes.label: Bayesian methods and sequential testing
nodes.text: Bayesian methods combine what you believed before the test (the prior) with the test results to produce an updated belief, and sequential testing lets you stop testing early once the evidence is clearly good or clearly bad.
aliases: In a sequential probability ratio test

nodes.label: Hypothesis testing basics (null hypothesis, significance, McNemar test)
nodes.text: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is too large to be a coincidence, by assuming at first that there is no real difference (the null hypothesis) and computing how surprising the data would then be.

nodes.label: Base rate and exposure-based rates (events per 1,000 hours)
nodes.text: A base rate is how often something happens in normal operation, and an exposure-based rate expresses it per unit of exposure, such as false alarms per 1,000 operating hours, rather than per staged test.

nodes.label: Weighting strata to a field rate
nodes.text: Weighting strata means combining the measured rate in each group of conditions (each stratum) into one overall rate by multiplying each by the share of real operating time that group represents.

nodes.label: The RAND argument
nodes.text: The RAND argument is the finding, from a 2016 report by the RAND Corporation (a research organization), that proving a self-driving car is as safe as a human driver by simply driving it would take hundreds of millions to billions of miles, far more than any fleet can drive.

nodes.label: Combining simulation and physical evidence
nodes.text: Combining simulation and physical evidence means using a large number of virtual runs to supply the statistical volume and a smaller number of physical tests to prove that the simulation can be trusted, so that the two together support a claim neither could support alone.

nodes.label: Keeping failure-seeking tests separate from performance estimates
nodes.text: Tests designed to find failures and tests designed to measure how often failures happen must be kept in separate pools with separate data and separate rules, because mixing them makes the measured rate wrong in one direction or the other.

nodes.label: Pre-registration
nodes.text: Pre-registration means writing down, before the data exist, exactly what will be claimed, how it will be measured, which samples will be used and when testing will stop, so that the analysis cannot be bent to fit the results.

nodes.label: Over-fitting
nodes.text: Over-fitting is what happens when a system's settings are adjusted so closely to the particular tests it was tuned on that it performs well on those tests and worse on anything new.

nodes.label: Hold-out set, tuning split and cross-validation
nodes.text: A hold-out set is a portion of the test data kept back and never used for tuning, a tuning split is the division of data into parts for tuning, confirming and auditing, and cross-validation is the practice of rotating which part is held out so that every part is used for checking once.

nodes.label: Performance baseline
nodes.text: A performance baseline is a careful measurement of how well the existing warning-only system performs, made before the new braking system is judged, so that "better" has something to be better than.

nodes.label: Fair comparison of old and new systems
nodes.text: A fair comparison judges the old warning system and the new braking system on the same hazards, in the same conditions, using the same yardstick, so that any difference is due to the systems and not to the circumstances.

nodes.label: Regression (a new version performing worse)
nodes.text: A regression is a case that used to pass and now fails after a change to the software or the settings, and regression testing is the habit of rerunning a fixed set of cases after every change to catch exactly that.

nodes.label: Key performance indicator (KPI) and metric
nodes.text: A metric is any quantity you measure, and a key performance indicator (KPI) is a metric that has been chosen, with a target value, to judge whether the system or the project is succeeding.

nodes.label: Constrained multi-objective optimization
nodes.text: Constrained multi-objective optimization is the task of choosing settings that do well on several goals at once (few misses, few false alarms, few unnecessary brakes, little lost production) while never violating certain hard limits.

nodes.label: Pareto front and trade-off
nodes.text: A trade-off is a situation where improving one goal worsens another, and the Pareto front is the set of settings where no goal can be improved any further without making some other goal worse.

nodes.label: Optimization methods named in the booklet (genetic algorithms, NSGA-II, Bayesian optimization, gradient-free search)
nodes.text: These are the search procedures the booklet names for finding good settings when the only way to judge a setting is to run it through a slow simulation and see what happens.
aliases: Optimization methods named in the booklet

nodes.label: Human factors as a tuning objective
nodes.text: Treating human factors as a tuning objective means counting the rate of unnecessary warnings and brakes as a safety goal in its own right, because operators who are interrupted too often stop trusting the system and start disabling it.

nodes.label: Transferring settings across machine models (physics-based parameterization, archetypes, partial pooling, transfer optimization)
nodes.text: Transferring settings means getting a braking system tuned on one machine model to work on another, with a different size, mass and sensor layout, by expressing the settings in physical terms that can be measured on each machine instead of re-tuning each one by hand.

nodes.label: Variant management
nodes.text: Variant management is the discipline of keeping track of every version of the machine, its sensors and its settings, so that the right evidence is attached to the right variant and a change to one does not silently invalidate another.

nodes.label: Data lineage and the independence rule
nodes.text: Data lineage is the recorded history of where every piece of data came from and what was done to it, and the independence rule says that the data used to judge a system must have had no part in building or tuning it.

nodes.label: Scenario description languages (OpenSCENARIO, DSL)
nodes.text: A scenario description language is a formal written format for describing a test situation (who is where, moving how, under what conditions) so that a computer can generate and run it, and a domain-specific language (DSL) is a small programming language built for one subject area.

nodes.label: Campaign (test campaign) and campaign architecture
nodes.text: A test campaign is a planned set of test runs executed together for one purpose, and the campaign architecture is the overall arrangement of campaigns, in time and by purpose, that turns a limited window into a defensible safety claim.

nodes.label: Credibility of a simulation
nodes.text: The credibility of a simulation is the degree to which a decision maker can trust its results enough to act on them, and it is earned with evidence, not with realistic-looking pictures.

nodes.label: Verification, validation and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ)
nodes.text: VVUQ is the three-part discipline of checking that a simulation program is built correctly (verification), that it matches the real world (validation), and how much its answers could still be wrong (uncertainty quantification).

nodes.label: Code verification versus solution verification
nodes.text: Code verification checks that the simulation software has no errors in how it solves its equations; solution verification estimates how much numerical error remains in one particular run.

nodes.label: Model validation versus model calibration
nodes.text: Calibration adjusts a model's parameters until it matches a set of measurements; validation tests whether the adjusted model then predicts measurements it has never seen, and doing both on the same data is cheating.

nodes.label: Context of use and question of interest
nodes.text: The question of interest is the exact decision a simulation is meant to inform, and the context of use is the precise role the simulation's output plays in making that decision.

nodes.label: Model risk: influence times consequence
nodes.text: Model risk is how much a simulation's output drives a decision (its influence) combined with how severe a wrong decision would be (the consequence), and it sets how much credibility evidence the simulation must have.

nodes.label: Credibility factors and credibility levels
nodes.text: Credibility factors are the separate aspects of a simulation that are each rated, and credibility levels are the 0 to 4 scale on which the NASA standard scores each factor, without adding the scores into one total.

nodes.label: Credible Simulation Process and simulation quality (ASAM QSQ)
nodes.text: The Credible Simulation Process is a German industry method for building credibility evidence into every step of a simulation project, and ASAM QSQ is a standardization project trying to define measurable simulation-quality metrics, still unfinished in 2026.
aliases: Credible Simulation Process and simulation quality

nodes.label: NASA-STD-7009 and NASA-HDBK-7009
nodes.text: NASA-STD-7009 is the US space agency's standard for models and simulations, written after the Columbia accident, and NASA-HDBK-7009 is its implementation handbook.

nodes.label: ASME V&V 10, V&V 20 and V&V 40
nodes.text: These are three standards from the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) on verification and validation: V&V 10 for structural models, V&V 20 for fluid-flow and heat-transfer models, and V&V 40 for judging model credibility by risk, written for medical devices.

nodes.label: FDA guidance on computational modeling for medical devices
nodes.text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published final guidance in November 2023 on assessing the credibility of computer models in medical-device submissions, and the booklet cites it as the clearest regulator-level statement of how to start from the decision rather than from the simulator.

nodes.label: Nuclear practice: EMDAP, PIRT and BEPU
nodes.text: EMDAP is the US nuclear regulator's 20-step process for building and judging a safety-analysis model, PIRT is its ranked list of the physical phenomena that matter most, and BEPU is the nuclear practice of reporting a best-estimate result with its uncertainty rather than a single worst-case number.
aliases: Evaluation Model Development and Assessment Process

nodes.label: Aerospace practice: FAA similarity rules, DO-178C, DO-330 and MIL-STD-3022
nodes.text: Aviation accepts simulation and prior evidence under strict rules: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lets a validated model cover similar designs and accepts service history for similar systems, DO-178C and DO-330 govern software and the tools that produce evidence, and MIL-STD-3022 is the US defense template for documenting model verification, validation and accreditation.

nodes.label: Rail practice: EN 14363 and DynoTRAIN
nodes.text: EN 14363 is the European rail standard for approving how a vehicle runs on track, and it is the one standard in the booklet that formally lets a validated simulation extend acceptance to new conditions and modified vehicles; DynoTRAIN is the research project that built its validation method.

nodes.label: Technology readiness level (TRL)
nodes.text: A technology readiness level is a 1 to 9 score of how mature a technology is, from a basic idea (TRL 1) to a system proven in real operation (TRL 9), defined for space systems in ISO 16290:2013.

nodes.label: Sim-to-real gap, measured
nodes.text: The measured sim-to-real gap is the difference between what a simulation produces and what the real sensor, machine or function produces in the same situation, expressed as a number with a stated metric and condition rather than as a general worry.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.text: In this field, correlation means the demonstrated agreement between a simulation and a physical test of the same situation, measured with agreed metrics; it is the act of anchoring the virtual world to the real one.

nodes.label: Scalar-output agreement
nodes.text: Scalar-output agreement compares one number from the simulation with the same number from the physical test, for example stopping distance or the time at which braking was triggered, usually as a percentage error with an agreed error band.

nodes.label: Time-history agreement
nodes.text: Time-history agreement compares a whole curve over time from the simulation with the same curve from the physical test, so that differences in timing and shape are caught, not only differences in the peak value.

nodes.label: Distributional agreement
nodes.text: Distributional agreement compares the whole spread of many simulated results with the whole spread of many measured results, which is needed when repeated runs of the same situation legitimately differ.

nodes.label: Image and field similarity metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, FID, mutual information)
nodes.text: These metrics score how much a simulated image, radar map or other field of values resembles a real one; they are useful for rendering quality but can disagree with whether a detector behaves the same on both.

nodes.label: Error metrics (MAE, MAPE, RMSE)
nodes.text: MAE, MAPE and RMSE are three standard ways to turn many individual simulation-versus-measurement differences into one average error figure.

nodes.label: Task-level gap versus pixel-level similarity
nodes.text: Pixel-level similarity asks whether a simulated sensor output looks like the real one; task-level gap asks whether the software that uses it (detector, tracker, braking logic) behaves the same on both, and a pretty image can still fail the second test.

nodes.label: Closed-loop agreement
nodes.text: Closed-loop agreement checks that, when the simulated braking system is allowed to act and the simulated machine responds, the outcome (when the brake fired, where the machine stopped, and whether it braked when it should not have) matches the real machine doing the same.

nodes.label: Tolerance and acceptance band
nodes.text: A tolerance, or acceptance band, is the amount of disagreement between simulation and physical test that is allowed before the model is judged not good enough for the decision it supports.

nodes.label: Uncertainty: aleatory versus epistemic
nodes.text: Aleatory uncertainty is natural randomness that no amount of study removes; epistemic uncertainty is lack of knowledge that more data or a better model could reduce, and the two must be tracked separately.

nodes.label: Sensitivity analysis
nodes.text: Sensitivity analysis changes a model's inputs, one or several at a time, to learn which of them most affect the output, so that effort, physical tests and worry go where they matter.

nodes.label: Validity envelope (domain of validity) and extrapolation
nodes.text: The validity envelope is the documented range of machines, sensors, conditions and scenarios within which a simulation has been validated against physical data; extrapolation is using the simulation outside that range, and it is where credibility fails fastest.

nodes.label: Validated parameter ranges and known model limits
nodes.text: Validated parameter ranges are the specific values of each input (speed, mass, mount height, visibility) between which a model has been checked against physical data, and known model limits are the documented places where it is known to be wrong, approximate or silent.

nodes.label: Held-out measurements and independent physical data
nodes.text: Held-out measurements are physical test results deliberately kept away from the people and processes that build and tune the model, so that they can later prove, rather than suggest, that the model predicts reality.

nodes.label: Deciding which physical tests to keep and which to replace
nodes.text: The decision follows information value and extrapolation risk, not a fixed percentage: physical tests stay where they anchor new physics, boundaries and high-consequence outcomes, and simulation fills the repetitive interior between those anchors.

nodes.label: Extending a validated model to another machine model or sensor position
nodes.text: A model validated on one machine is extended to another by showing what changed, whether the change can affect a validated phenomenon, and what targeted bridging tests close the gap; it is never inherited automatically.

nodes.label: Using the existing warning system's field history as a reference
nodes.text: The years of recorded operation of the current warning system can validate the simulation's inputs and some of its submodels, but not the new closed-loop braking chain, and only if three traps are respected.

nodes.label: False confidence from simulation
nodes.text: False confidence is trusting a result more than its evidence justifies, and the booklet documents three ways it happens: using a model outside its data, choosing a metric that hides the error, and relying on a test protocol that never sampled the dangerous condition.

nodes.label: Simulation specialist's objections
nodes.text: In the booklet's hostile review, the simulation specialist's objections reduce to three: the model is unvalidated, the simulator architecture is being frozen against assumed hardware, and metrics risk being chosen for convenience after the fact.

nodes.label: The credibility package (what a safety board or outside assessor expects to see)
nodes.text: The credibility package is the full set of documents an internal safety board or external assessor needs before relying on simulation evidence, and it contains far more than simulator results.

nodes.label: Independent review of the test plan
nodes.text: Independent review of the test plan is having people who did not write the plan, and who do not need it to succeed, examine what will be tested, how, with which metrics and thresholds, before the tests begin.

nodes.label: Standard
nodes.text: A standard is a written agreement, produced by a committee of experts, that says how something should be made, tested or described so that everyone means the same thing.

nodes.label: Standards bodies (ISO, IEC, CEN, CENELEC, ASAM, SAE, IEEE, UL and national bodies)
nodes.text: Standards bodies are the organizations that run the committees, hold the votes and publish the standards.
aliases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers

nodes.label: Technical committee ISO/TC 127 and how a standard is numbered
nodes.text: ISO/TC 127 is the ISO committee for earth-moving machinery, and the numbers, parts and years in a standard's name tell you exactly which document and which edition is meant.

nodes.label: Stage codes (TS, PAS, TR, DIS, FDIS, PRF, under revision, under publication)
nodes.text: Stage codes are the labels that tell you how far a standard has traveled from first draft to published text, and whether the published text is about to change.

nodes.label: Regulation, directive, law and guidance note
nodes.text: A law is a rule the state can enforce, a regulation and a directive are two forms that European Union law takes, and a guidance note is official advice that explains how to comply without itself being law.

nodes.label: Harmonized standard, presumption of conformity and state of the art
nodes.text: A harmonized standard is one that European law officially lists, so that a product built to it is presumed to meet the law, and "state of the art" is the legal phrase for the level of safety that current good practice makes possible.

nodes.label: Type approval, self-certification and conformity assessment
nodes.text: Conformity assessment is the process of checking that a product meets the rules; type approval and self-certification are two ways of doing it, an authority checking a sample and issuing an approval, or the manufacturer checking and declaring for itself.

nodes.label: CE marking and notified body
nodes.text: CE marking is the label a manufacturer puts on a product to declare that it meets European Union law, and a notified body is an independent organization appointed by the authorities to check high-risk products before that label may be applied.

nodes.label: Test method (test object, distance, speed, condition, pass criterion)
nodes.text: A test method, as a standard or regulation defines it, is the exact recipe for one test: what object to use, where to place it, how fast to drive, under what conditions, and what result counts as a pass.

nodes.label: ISO 21815 series (collision warning and avoidance)
nodes.text: ISO 21815 is the family of international standards that says what a collision warning or collision avoidance system on an earth-moving machine must do, how it talks to the machine, and how to work out the distance at which it must act.

nodes.label: ISO 19014 series (functional safety for earth-moving machinery)
nodes.text: ISO 19014 is the family of standards that tells a maker of earth-moving machines how to make sure the electronic control system behind a safety function, such as an automatic brake, is designed, built, tested and programmed so that its faults do not cause harm.

nodes.label: ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 (brake performance)
nodes.text: ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 are the standards that say how well the brakes of an earth-moving machine must work and how to test them, ISO 3450 for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines and ISO 10265 for slow crawler machines.

nodes.label: ISO 16001 and ISO 5006 (object detection, visibility aids and operator visibility)
nodes.text: ISO 16001 sets performance requirements and tests for the systems that detect objects and help the operator see around an earth-moving machine, and ISO 5006 defines how the operator's own field of view is measured.

nodes.label: ISO 17757 and ISO 19296 (autonomous machine safety and underground mining machines)
nodes.text: ISO 17757 is the safety standard for autonomous and semi-autonomous earth-moving and mining machine systems, and ISO 19296 is the general safety standard for mobile machines that work underground.

nodes.label: ISO 6165 and ISO 20474 / EN 474 (classification and general safety of earth-moving machinery)
nodes.text: ISO 6165 defines which machines count as earth-moving machinery, and ISO 20474 and its European twin EN 474 set the general safety requirements that every such machine must meet.

nodes.label: ISO 15998 and ISO 13766 (withdrawn control-system standard and EMC)
