nodes.text: ISO 15998 was the former functional-safety standard for electronic machine-control systems on earth-moving machinery, withdrawn in 2022 and replaced by ISO 19014, and ISO 13766 is the standard for electromagnetic compatibility of such machines.

nodes.label: ISO 12100, ISO 13849, IEC 62061 and IEC 61508 (the machinery and functional-safety family)
nodes.text: These four standards form the general toolkit for making any machine safe: ISO 12100 for assessing and reducing risk, ISO 13849 and IEC 62061 for the safety of control systems on machinery, and IEC 61508 as the parent standard for electronic safety systems in every industry.

nodes.label: IEC 61496, IEC TS 62998, ISO 3691-4 and ISO 18497 (safety sensors, driverless industrial trucks and agricultural automation)
nodes.text: These are neighboring standards from other sectors: IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 certify safety sensors in factories, ISO 3691-4 covers driverless warehouse trucks, and ISO 18497 covers automated farm machines, including how to test their obstacle detection.
aliases: IEC 61496, IEC TS 62998, ISO 3691-4 and ISO 18497

nodes.label: ISO 21448, ISO 26262 and the AI safety standards (ISO/PAS 8800, ISO/IEC TR 5469, ISO/IEC 42001, 23894, 24029)
nodes.text: ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 are the road-vehicle standards for functional safety and for safety when sensors and software misjudge a situation without failing, and the ISO/PAS 8800 and ISO/IEC documents are the first, mostly unfinished, attempts to write standards for machine learning in safety functions.
aliases: ISO 21448, ISO 26262 and the AI safety standards

nodes.label: ISO 34501 to 34505, ISO/PAS 34506, ISO/TS 5083 and ISO 19206 (scenario-based evaluation and test targets)
nodes.text: The ISO 3450x series and ISO/TS 5083 are road-vehicle standards for describing, sorting and choosing the test scenarios of an automated driving system, and ISO 19206 defines the dummies and foam cars that stand in for people and vehicles in crash-avoidance tests.
aliases: ISO 34501 to 34505, ISO/PAS 34506, ISO/TS 5083 and ISO 19206

nodes.label: ISO 18571, ISO 16290 and ISO 25119
nodes.text: ISO 18571 defines a score for how closely two curves agree, ISO 16290 defines the technology readiness levels, and ISO 25119 is the functional-safety standard for control systems on farm machines.

nodes.label: Systems and software engineering standards (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, 29119, 42010, 15026-2, IEEE 1012, ISO 31000, IEC 31010)
nodes.text: These are the general standards for how to run an engineering project: how to organize a system's life cycle, document tests, describe an architecture, write an assurance case, verify and validate, and manage risk.

nodes.label: Rail and aviation standards (EN 50126 to EN 50129, EN 50716, EN 14363, DO-178C, DO-330, DO-385, ED-256)
nodes.text: These are the safety and simulation standards of two industries, railways and aviation, that have accepted simulation as evidence for longer than road or off-road vehicles have.

nodes.label: UL 4600 (autonomous products safety case)
nodes.text: UL 4600 is a standard that tells a developer what a complete safety case for an autonomous product must cover, in the form of long lists of questions and claims to be answered with evidence.

nodes.label: UN regulations (UN R152, R131, R159, R171) and UNECE WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM
nodes.text: The UN regulations are the shared road-vehicle approval rules written at the United Nations in Geneva, R131 and R152 for emergency braking on trucks and cars, R159 for moving-off information and R171 for driver assistance, and WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM are the forum, working party, expert group and method that produce them.
aliases: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe

nodes.label: FMVSS 127, NHTSA, NTSB and IIHS
nodes.text: FMVSS 127 is the United States rule requiring automatic emergency braking on new cars, NHTSA is the agency that writes such rules and investigates defects, NTSB is the independent board that investigates accidents, and IIHS is the insurer-funded institute that tests and rates vehicles.

nodes.label: Euro NCAP and its virtual-testing protocol
nodes.text: Euro NCAP is the European consumer program that crash-tests cars and awards star ratings, and its virtual-testing protocol is the first published procedure under which an outside assessor accepts a manufacturer's simulation results for crash avoidance, subject to correlation and random physical checks.

nodes.label: EU Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, the AI Act, the Product Liability Directive and the Data Act
nodes.text: These four European Union laws set the legal ground for a machine sold in Europe from 2027: the Machinery Regulation governs its safety and conformity, the AI Act and its 2026 amendment govern artificial intelligence in it, the Product Liability Directive governs who pays when it causes harm, and the Data Act governs access to the data it produces.

nodes.label: United Kingdom rules (HSE, Supply of Machinery Regulations, UKCA)
nodes.text: In Great Britain the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) enforces workplace safety, the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 govern what machines may be sold, and UKCA is the British conformity mark that replaced CE marking after the United Kingdom left the European Union.

nodes.label: United States rules (OSHA 29 CFR 1926.601, MSHA 30 CFR, NIOSH)
nodes.text: In the United States, OSHA writes and enforces construction safety rules, MSHA does the same for mines, and NIOSH is the research institute whose studies and tests inform both; none of their rules requires automatic braking.

nodes.label: Canada and Australia rules (CSA M424, WHS laws, NSW Resources Regulator, RSHQ QGN 27 and QGN 33, DMIRS)
nodes.text: Canada regulates mining province by province with CSA M424 as the relevant national standard, and Australia uses model Work Health and Safety laws plus state mining regulators in New South Wales, Queensland and Western Australia, none of which mandates automatic braking.

nodes.label: South Africa rules (MHSA, DMRE, Chapter 8 regulations, MOSH, CPS verification specifications)
nodes.text: South Africa is the only country the booklet found that legally requires automatic slow-down and braking on mining machines, through regulations under the Mine Health and Safety Act, with the industry's MOSH specifications and independent test regime filling in the numbers the law leaves out.

nodes.label: South America and Asia rules (NR-22, NR-12, DS 132, SERNAGEOMIN, DS 024-2016-EM, DGMS, GB standards, JARI)
nodes.text: Brazil, Chile, Peru, India, China and Japan each have general mining or machinery safety rules, and in none of them did the booklet find a dedicated rule with numeric tests for automatic braking on off-road machines.

nodes.label: EMESRT and PR-5A (Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table, vehicle interaction performance requirement)
nodes.text: EMESRT is a group of mining companies that writes shared safety requirements for the makers of mining machines, and PR-5A is its requirement for controlling collisions between vehicles and people, which gives the industry its nine-layer model of controls and its catalog of collision scenarios.

nodes.label: ICMM, the nine-layer control model and the ICSV program (International Council on Mining and Metals, Innovation for Cleaner Safer Vehicles)
nodes.text: ICMM is the international association of the largest mining companies, and its Innovation for Cleaner, Safer Vehicles program set the industry goal of making collision avoidance technology available by 2025, using EMESRT's nine-layer model of controls.
aliases: ICMM, the nine-layer control model and the ICSV program

nodes.label: ACARP and its two-tier test approach (Australian Coal Association Research Program)
nodes.text: ACARP is the research fund of the Australian coal industry, and its project C26028 proposed a two-tier framework for testing proximity detection systems: first prove that the system detects objects, then prove that its advisory or intervention action works.
aliases: ACARP and its two-tier test approach

nodes.label: MOSH and its TRL stage gates (Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health learning hub)
nodes.text: MOSH is the learning hub of the Minerals Council South Africa that turned the country's automatic-braking law into engineering specifications and a staged, independently verified test regime organized by technology readiness level.
aliases: Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health
MOSH and its TRL stage gates

nodes.label: NIOSH, MSHA, BLS and CPWR (US bodies that publish accident data)
nodes.text: These four United States bodies produce the accident statistics the booklet relies on: NIOSH researches workplace safety, MSHA regulates mines and records their accidents, BLS counts all workplace deaths and injuries, and CPWR analyzes the construction figures.
aliases: US bodies that publish accident data

nodes.label: WorkSafe New Zealand, WorkSafe Western Australia (SIR 286), HSE and EU-OSHA
nodes.text: These are workplace-safety regulators and agencies whose incident reports and statistics the booklet uses: WorkSafe New Zealand for mines and quarries, WorkSafe Western Australia for the Significant Incident Reports on autonomous haul trucks, Britain's HSE for national figures, and EU-OSHA, the European agency, mainly as a source of legislation summaries.
aliases: WorkSafe New Zealand, WorkSafe Western Australia

nodes.label: PEGASUS, VVM, SET Level, VaViM and EVIDENT (German and European research programs on scenario-based validation)
nodes.text: These are the publicly funded research programs, mostly German and Swedish, that worked out how to validate automated driving with scenarios and simulation, and whose durations show how long building such a capability takes.
aliases: PEGASUS, VVM, SET Level, VaViM and EVIDENT

nodes.label: Waymo and Motional collision-avoidance validation methods (on-road precedents)
nodes.text: Waymo and Motional are developers of self-driving road vehicles whose published safety methods show how simulation, replay, closed-course tests, public roads and shadow mode are layered, and whose material the booklet treats as vendor evidence from on-road.
aliases: Waymo and Motional collision-avoidance validation methods

nodes.label: Auto-GCAS (Automatic Ground Collision Avoidance System for fighter aircraft)
nodes.text: Auto-GCAS is the system on F-16 and F-35 fighter aircraft that takes control and pulls the aircraft up when it is about to fly into the ground, a precedent for an automatic intervention that had to be proven both effective and free of nuisance activations.

nodes.label: ACAS X and TCAS (aircraft collision avoidance, encounter models)
nodes.text: TCAS is the long-standing system that warns airline pilots of a possible mid-air collision and tells them to climb or descend, ACAS X is its successor, and the encounter model is the statistical description of near-collisions that let ACAS X be validated largely by simulation.

nodes.label: Honda CMBS investigations (NHTSA PE22-003, EA24-002, EA25-002) as a precedent for unnecessary braking
nodes.text: The Honda investigations are the United States regulator's inquiries into cars whose Collision Mitigation Braking System braked hard with nothing in the way, the largest documented case of unnecessary automatic braking reaching a production fleet.

nodes.label: Rail, port, forklift and agriculture precedents (Wabtec and others)
nodes.text: These are the neighboring industries the booklet searched for cases of automatic braking validated with less physical testing, and in each it found products on the market but no published validation method, duration or share of physical testing.
aliases: Rail, port, forklift and agriculture precedents

nodes.label: The Pretoria process and MineSim (mining research precedents)
nodes.text: The Pretoria process is the University of Pretoria's step-by-step method for independently verifying mining collision-avoidance systems, and MineSim is an open-source simulation test system for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines.

nodes.label: RAND Corporation and GAO (the Driving to Safety report and the US Government Accountability Office cost and schedule guides)
nodes.text: RAND is an independent American research institute whose 2016 report showed that road miles alone cannot prove a self-driving car is safe, and GAO is the audit arm of the United States Congress whose guides and program reviews show what makes cost and schedule estimates credible.

nodes.label: DARPA RACER program (off-road autonomy research)
nodes.text: RACER is a program of the United States defense research agency DARPA to make military ground vehicles drive themselves fast across rough off-road terrain, and its simulation arm built a very large virtual off-road environment.

nodes.label: Columbia Accident Investigation Board (why a space shuttle accident appears in a mining booklet)
nodes.text: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board was the body that investigated the loss of the space shuttle Columbia in 2003, and its findings about a computer model used far outside the range it had been tested on are the textbook case of false confidence from simulation.

nodes.label: Tool chain
nodes.text: A tool chain is the set of separate software programs and hardware boxes that are connected together so that one virtual test can run from start to finish.

nodes.label: Complete and near-complete simulation platforms
nodes.text: A complete simulation platform is a commercial or open-source product that tries to cover several layers of the tool chain at once: scenarios, environments, sensors, vehicle motion and test execution.

nodes.label: Open-source simulators
nodes.text: An open-source simulator is a simulation program whose source code anyone may read, change and use without paying a license fee, under conditions set by its license.

nodes.label: Sensor simulation tools
nodes.text: A sensor simulation tool produces artificial camera images, radar returns, lidar point clouds or ultrasonic echoes from a virtual scene, so the braking software can be tested without a real sensor.

nodes.label: Vehicle and machine dynamics tools
nodes.text: A vehicle and machine dynamics tool calculates how a machine moves: how it accelerates, steers, tips, sinks into soft ground and stops when the brakes act.

nodes.label: Terrain and soil tools
nodes.text: Terrain and soil tools calculate how the ground deforms under a machine, how a bucket digs into a pile and how loose material flows, because soft ground changes how a machine stops.

nodes.label: Environment creation and reconstruction tools
nodes.text: Environment creation and reconstruction tools build the three-dimensional virtual job site, either by designing it by hand and by rules or by rebuilding a real site from photographs, laser scans and machine recordings.

nodes.label: Scenario generation and test management tools
nodes.text: Scenario generation tools describe and vary the test situations; test management tools decide which runs to execute, run them, and keep track of the results.

nodes.label: Data replay and HIL hardware
nodes.text: Data replay feeds recorded real sensor data back into the braking software, and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) hardware is the real-time computer and signal equipment that lets the real control unit run against a simulated machine.
aliases: CPU with a field-programmable gate array

nodes.label: Operator-in-the-loop simulators
nodes.text: An operator-in-the-loop simulator is a cab, screens and controls where a real person drives a simulated machine, so that human reactions to warnings and automatic braking can be measured.

nodes.label: Cloud execution services
nodes.text: Cloud execution means renting computers, including graphics processors, by the hour over the internet instead of buying them, so that thousands of simulations can run in parallel.

nodes.label: Mining, construction, agriculture and forestry specific tools
nodes.text: These are the few simulation tools, datasets and frameworks that were built for, or deliberately adapted to, off-road working machines rather than road cars.

nodes.label: Engineering service companies and research institutes
nodes.text: Engineering service companies sell engineering work by the hour or by the project, and research institutes sell applied research, test facilities and independent assessment; both can do parts of virtual validation for a manufacturer.

nodes.label: Build, buy or partner
nodes.text: Build, buy or partner is the decision between writing the simulation capability in-house on open-source parts, buying commercial products, or paying an outside company to deliver it.

nodes.label: License types and pricing models
nodes.text: A software license is the permission to use a program under stated conditions, and the pricing model is how the vendor charges for it: per computer, per shared pool, per year, per person, or not at all.

nodes.label: The three example tool chains at different cost levels
nodes.text: The booklet sketches three ways to assemble a tool chain, from an open-source core to a fully commercial chain with a partner, and labels them lowest, middle and highest by relative cost and integration posture, not by dollar figures.
aliases: Speedgoat or NI for later hardware-in-the-loop
three example tool chains at different cost levels

nodes.label: CPU, GPU, FPGA, VRAM and real-time computers
nodes.text: These are the kinds of computing hardware a simulation program needs: the central processor for general work, the graphics processor for massively parallel work, the programmable chip for exact timing, the graphics memory that holds the scene, and computers built to answer on a fixed schedule.

nodes.label: Graphics cards named in the booklet
nodes.text: A graphics card is a circuit board carrying a graphics processing unit (GPU) and its memory, and the booklet names specific models because the speed of sensor simulation depends heavily on which one is used.

nodes.label: High-performance computing (HPC) and cluster, versus workstation
nodes.text: A workstation is one powerful desktop computer; a cluster is many computers wired together and managed as one; high-performance computing (HPC) is the largest class of cluster, built for scientific calculation.

nodes.label: Compute cost and run time
nodes.text: Compute cost is what it costs to run the simulations, and it is set by three numbers: the price per hour of the computer, how many hours it runs, and how much simulated time each hour produces.

nodes.label: Software terms a planner meets
nodes.text: These are the everyday words of software work that appear throughout the booklet: how programs talk to each other, which programming tools the simulators use, and how teams package, track and automatically test their code.

nodes.label: Data storage, data lineage and record keeping for thousands of runs
nodes.text: Record keeping for simulation means storing, for every one of thousands of runs, exactly what was run, with which versions and inputs, and where every input came from, so that any result can be reproduced and defended later.

nodes.label: Project plan, work package and deliverable
nodes.text: A project plan says what will be done, by whom and by when; a work package is one bounded chunk of that work; a deliverable is the concrete thing a work package hands over.

nodes.label: Gantt chart, milestone and dependency
nodes.text: A Gantt chart is a calendar drawing in which each task is a horizontal bar from its start to its finish, a milestone is a single dated event with no duration, and a dependency is the rule that one task cannot start until another has finished.

nodes.label: Critical path and buffer
nodes.text: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks in a plan, so any delay on it delays the end date; a buffer is spare time deliberately placed in the plan to absorb such delays.

nodes.label: Planning fallacy, reference class forecasting and P50 / P80 estimates
nodes.text: The planning fallacy is the proven human habit of underestimating how long one's own work will take; reference class forecasting corrects it by looking at how long similar past projects actually took; and P50 and P80 dates state the finish date with a 50% and an 80% chance of being met.

nodes.label: Schedule risk analysis and Monte Carlo schedule simulation
nodes.text: Schedule risk analysis gives every task a range of possible durations instead of one number, and a Monte Carlo schedule simulation runs the whole plan thousands of times with random draws from those ranges to find how likely each finish date is.

nodes.label: Risk register, assumption log and unknowns (known unknowns)
nodes.text: A risk register lists the uncertain events that could hurt the plan, an assumption log lists the propositions the plan currently depends on, and the unknowns list records the questions the team knows it cannot yet answer.
aliases: Risk register, assumption log and unknowns

nodes.label: Pre-mortem, red team and expert review (Delphi method, expert elicitation)
nodes.text: A pre-mortem imagines the project has already failed and asks why; a red team is a group charged with attacking the plan; expert review, including the Delphi method and structured elicitation, is a disciplined way of collecting and weighing what specialists believe.
aliases: Pre-mortem, red team and expert review

nodes.label: Stage gate, evidence gate and go or no-go decision
nodes.text: A stage gate is a formal decision point between phases of a project, an evidence gate is one whose pass criterion is demonstrated knowledge rather than a date, and a go or no-go decision is the choice made there to continue, restrict, change course or stop.

nodes.label: Pilot, proof of concept and minimum viable product (MVP)
nodes.text: A proof of concept shows that something can work at all, a pilot tests whether the approach is feasible on a small but real slice, and a minimum viable product (MVP) is the smallest deliverable that is still useful.
aliases: Pilot, proof of concept and minimum viable product

nodes.label: Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) and integrated test planning
nodes.text: A Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) is the single overarching document that ties every planned test, virtual or physical, to the decision it informs, the data it needs, its resources, its schedule and its pass criteria.

nodes.label: PMBOK, PMI, PRINCE2 and agile
nodes.text: PMBOK, PRINCE2 and agile are general frameworks for how to run projects: two are published bodies of project-management method, and agile is a family of practices that delivers work in short, repeated cycles.

nodes.label: Cost estimating and schedule guides (GAO guides, AACE)
nodes.text: These are published handbooks on how to build a cost estimate and a project schedule that can withstand audit, written by the United States Government Accountability Office (GAO) and by AACE International, a professional association for cost engineering.

nodes.label: Bottom line up front (BLUF) and the one-page summary
nodes.text: Bottom line up front (BLUF) is the writing rule that the conclusion and the decision requested come first, and the one-page summary is the document that applies it so an executive can grasp the decision, the confidence and the risks in a page or two.

nodes.label: PR/FAQ (working backwards) and other presentation formats
nodes.text: PR/FAQ is a planning document written as the press release and the questions-and-answers that would accompany a finished product, and it is one of several named formats for presenting a plan to decision makers and expert reviewers.

nodes.label: Visuals that work
nodes.text: Visuals that work are the drawings in a plan that expose dependencies and gaps, rather than decorate; the booklet found no format proven to increase reviewer trust and recommends a division of labor among six kinds.

nodes.label: Request for proposal (RFP), non-disclosure agreement (NDA), statement of work, and supplier information
nodes.text: A request for proposal (RFP) asks vendors to propose a solution and a price, a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) lets two companies share secrets safely, a statement of work spells out exactly what a supplier will deliver, and supplier information is the technical data a sensor or tool vendor must hand over for a simulation to represent its product.
aliases: OSI as a Functional Mock-up Unit

nodes.label: Total cost of ownership, capital versus operating cost, full-time equivalent (FTE)
nodes.text: Total cost of ownership is everything a capability costs over its life, not just the purchase price; capital cost is money spent once on things that last, operating cost is money spent every month to keep running; and a full-time equivalent (FTE) is the work of one person for one full year.
aliases: Total cost of ownership, capital versus operating cost, full-time equivalent

nodes.label: Team and skills needed
nodes.text: The team and skills needed are the distinct specialist disciplines a manufacturer must have in place at the same time to build and defend a virtual validation capability.

nodes.label: Cheapest early experiments
nodes.text: The cheapest early experiments are small tests that can start immediately, with existing data and one machine, and are designed to prove the proposal wrong before expensive infrastructure is built.

nodes.label: Executive reviewer, finance reviewer, product liability reviewer
nodes.text: These are three of the skeptical readers the plan must satisfy, each needing a different view of the same evidence: the executive decides, the finance reviewer checks the money, and the product liability reviewer checks what would survive in court.
